title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
The results of \cite{BNOT16,BOT14,BKT16} are obtained in the stronger
form of density estimates by using the Malliavin calculus. The corresponding

title: Theorem A
body_md:
Suppose that the vector
fields are of class $C_{b}^{\infty}$ and satisfy the uniform ellipticity
condition (\ref{eq:UE}).

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) Let $H\in(1/2,1).$ There exist positive
constants $C_{1},C_{2}$ such that 

\[
\mathbb{P}(|X_{1}-x_{0}|>R)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2H+1}}
\]
for all large $R.$ 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Let $H\in(1/4,1/2)$. There exist positive
constants $C_{1},C_{2}$ such that \begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}(|X_{1}-x_{0}|>R)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2}}\label{eq:GenLowRoughIntro}
\end{equation}
for all large $R$.
head: environment

title: Theorem B
body_md:
There are examples of uniformly
elliptic systems $X_{t}$ with $C_{b}^{\infty}$-coefficients driven
by fBM with Hurst parameter $H\in(1/2,1)$, such that 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(|X_{1}-x_{0}|>R\big)\leqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2H+1}}
\]
for all large $R$.

title: Theorem D
body_md:
Let $\{V_{1},V_{2}\}$
be smooth, uniformly elliptic vector fields on the torus $\mathbb{T}^{2}=\mathbb{R}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}^{2}$.
Let $X_{t}$ be the solution to the SDE 
\[
dX_{t}=\tilde{V}_{1}(X_{t})dB_{t}^{1}+\tilde{V}_{2}(X_{t})dB_{t}^{2},\quad X_{0}=x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{2},
\]
where $(B_{t}^{1},B_{t}^{2})$ is a 2D fBM with Hurst parameter $H\in(1/2,1)$
and $\tilde{V}_{i}$ is the periodic extension of $V_{i}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{2}$
($i=1,2$). Then there exist positive constants $C_{1},C_{2},$ such
that 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(|X_{1}-x_{0}|>R\big)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2}}
\]
for all large $R$.

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
A $d$-dimensional \textit{fractional Brownian motion} (fBM) with
Hurst parameter $H\in(0,1)$ is an $\mathbb{R}^{d}$-valued stochastic
process $B_{t}=(B_{t}^{1},\cdots,B_{t}^{d})$ ($t\geqslant0$) which
satisfies the following properties.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) $B_{0}=0$ a.s.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) $B_{t}$ is a centered Gaussian process
whose covariance structure is given by 
\[
\mathbb{E}\big[B_{s}^{i}B_{t}^{j}\big]=R(s,t)\delta_{ij},\quad s,t\in[0,1],\ i,j=1,\cdots,d,
\]
where 
\[
R(s,t)=\frac{1}{2}\big(s^{2H}+t^{2H}-|s-t|^{2H}\big).
\]
(iii) $B_{t}$ has continuous sample paths a.s.
head: environment

label: eq:CMRep
title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
Let $\bar{{\cal H}}$ be the space of elements $h\in{\cal W}$ which
can be expressed as 
\begin{equation}
h_{t}=\mathbb{E}[B_{t}Z],\quad0\leqslant t\leqslant1\label{eq:CMRep}
\end{equation}
for some $Z\in{\cal C}_{1}$. The space $\bar{{\cal H}}$ is equipped
with an inner product structure which is defined by 
\[
\langle h_{1},h_{2}\rangle_{\bar{{\cal H}}}:=\mathbb{E}[Z_{1}Z_{2}],\quad h_{1},h_{2}\in\bar{{\cal H}},
\]
where $Z_{i}$ is the element of ${\cal C}_{1}$ representing $h_{i}$
through (\ref{eq:CMRep}) ($i=1,2$). The Hilbert space $(\bar{{\cal H}},\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\bar{{\cal H}}})$
is called the (intrinsic) \textit{Cameron-Martin space} of the fBM.
head: environment

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
Let $f$ be a function defined on $[0,1]$ and let $\alpha>0.$ Its
\textit{left fractional integral} of order $\alpha$ is defined by
\[
(I_{0^{+}}^{\alpha}f)(t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}f(s)(t-s)^{\alpha-1}ds,\quad0\leqslant t\leqslant1.
\]
Its \textit{left fractional derivative} of order $\alpha$ is defined
by 
\[
(D_{0^{+}}^{\alpha}f)(t):=\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big)^{[\alpha]+1}\big(I_{0^{+}}^{1-\{\alpha\}}f\big)(t),\quad0\leqslant t\leqslant1,
\]
where $[\alpha]$ is the integer part of $\alpha$ and $\{\alpha\}:=\alpha-[\alpha]$.

label: eq:Equiv2
title: Proof
body_md:
(i) The equivalence 
\[
\|h\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}\asymp_{H}\|D_{0^{+}}^{H-1/2}\dot{h}\|_{L^{2}([0,1])}
\]
is contained in \cite[Theorem 19]{Pic10} (with obvious restriction
from $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ to $[0,1]$). The equivalence 
\begin{equation}
\|D_{0^{+}}^{H-1/2}u\|_{L^{2}([0,1])}^{2}\asymp_{H}\|u\|_{L^{2}([0,1])}^{2}+\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{|u_{t}-u_{s}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{2H}}dsdt\label{eq:Equiv2}
\end{equation}
on $I_{0^{+}}^{H-1/2}(L^{2}([0,1]))$ requires some effort which we
now address. We set $\mu:=H-1/2$. It is important to note that $\mu\in(0,1/2)$.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) We claim that $I_{0+}^{\mu}:L^{2}([0,1])\rightarrow L^{2}([0,1])$
is a bounded linear operator, i.e. 
\begin{equation}
\|I_{0+}^{\mu}f\|_{2}\leqslant C_{\mu}\|f\|_{2}.\label{eq:CtyImu}
\end{equation}
Indeed, one can write $I_{0+}^{\mu}f=k_{\mu}*f$ where 
\[
k_{\mu}(t):=\frac{t^{\mu-1}}{\Gamma(\mu)}{\bf 1}_{(0,1)}(t).
\]
The estimate (\ref{eq:CtyImu}) follows from Young's convolution inequality
with $C_{\mu}:=\|k_{\mu}\|_{1}.$ Equivalently, one has 
\[
\|f\|_{2}\leqslant C_{\mu}\|D_{0^{+}}^{\mu}f\|_{2}
\]
for all $f\in I_{0^{+}}^{\mu}(L^{2}([0,1]))$. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iii) Define the following norms (cf. \cite{ER06}):
\[
\|f\|_{J^{\mu}(0,1)}:=\|f\|_{L^{2}([0,1])}+\|D_{0^{+}}^{\mu}f\|_{L^{2}([0,1])},\quad f\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,1));
\]
\[
\|g\|_{H^{\mu}(\mathbb{R})}:=\|g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}+\|[\omega\mapsto|\omega|^{\mu}\hat{g}(\omega)]\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})},\quad g\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}),
\]
where $\hat{g}$ denotes the Fourier transform of $g$. Let $J_{0}^{\mu}(0,1)$ (respectively, $H^{\mu}(0,1)$)
be the closure of $C_{c}^{\infty}((0,1))$ under $\|\cdot\|_{J^{\mu}(0,1)}$ (respectively, $\|\cdot\|_{H^{\mu}(\mathbb{R})}$; here functions on $(0,1)$ are
extended by zero to the whole $\mathbb{R}$). According to \cite[Theorem 2.13]{ER06},
one has $J_{0}^{\mu}(0,1)=H^{\mu}(0,1)$ and the two norms $\|\cdot\|_{J^{\mu}(0,1)}$,
$\|\cdot\|_{H^{\mu}(\mathbb{R})}$ are equivalent. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iv) We claim that 
\begin{equation}
J_{0}^{\mu}(0,1)=I_{0^{+}}^{\mu}(L^{2}([0,1])),\label{eq:J0JEq}
\end{equation}
where the latter space is equipped with the same norm. One only needs
to show that $I_{0^{+}}^{\mu}(L^{2}([0,1]))\subseteq J_{0}^{\mu}(0,1)$
as the other direction is trivial. To this end, let $u=I_{0^{+}}^{\mu}f$
with some $f\in L^{2}([0,1])$. Pick a sequence $f_{n}\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,1))$
with $f_{n}\rightarrow f$ in $L^{2}$ and set $v_{n}:=I_{0^{+}}^{\mu}f_{n}$.
By (\ref{eq:CtyImu}), one has $v_{n}\rightarrow u$ under $\|\cdot\|_{J^{\mu}(0,1)}$. 

It remains to show that $v_{n}\in J_{0}^{\mu}(0,1)$. Indeed, given
small $\varepsilon>0$, let $\chi_{\varepsilon}\in C^{\infty}([0,1])$
be such that 
\[
\chi_{\varepsilon}(t)=1\quad\text{for }t\leqslant1-2\varepsilon,\quad\chi_{\varepsilon}(t)=0\quad\text{for }t\geqslant1-\varepsilon.
\]
\[0\leqslant \chi_\varepsilon\leqslant 1,\quad |\dot{\chi}_\varepsilon|\leqslant C\varepsilon^{-1}.\]
Define $v_{n,\varepsilon}:=\chi_{\varepsilon}v_{n}\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,1))$
and set 
\[
w_{n,\varepsilon}:=v_{n}-v_{n,\varepsilon}=(1-\chi_{\varepsilon})v_{n}.
\]
It is apparent that $\|w_{n,\varepsilon}\|_{2}\rightarrow0$ as $\varepsilon\rightarrow0^{+}$
($n$ is fixed). In addition, since 
\[
\|\dot{w}_{n,\varepsilon}\|_{\infty}\leqslant\frac{C_{v_{n}}}{\varepsilon}\quad\text{and}\quad w_{n,\varepsilon}(t)=0\ \text{for }t\leqslant1-2\varepsilon,
\]
explicit calculation based on the formula (\ref{eq:FracDer}) shows
that 
\[
\|D_{0^{+}}^{\mu}w_{n,\varepsilon}\|_{2}\leqslant C_{\mu,v_{n}}\varepsilon^{1/2-\mu}.
\]
Since $\mu\in(0,1/2),$ it follows that $\|D_{0^{+}}^{\mu}w_{n,\varepsilon}\|_{2}\rightarrow0$
as $\varepsilon\rightarrow0^{+}$. Consequently, $v_{n,\varepsilon}\rightarrow v_{n}$
under $\|\cdot\|_{J^{\mu}(0,1)}$ and thus $v_{n}\in J_{0}^{\mu}(0,1)$.
One therefore concludes that $J_{0}^{\mu}(0,1)=I_{0^{+}}^{\mu}(L^{2}([0,1]))$. 

As a consequence of Parts (ii), (iii) and the relation (\ref{eq:J0JEq}), one arrives at the
following equivalence of norms 
\[
\|D_{0^{+}}^{\mu}u\|_{L^{2}([0,1])}\asymp_{H}\|\tilde{u}\|_{H^{\mu}(\mathbb{R})}
\]
for all $u\in I_{0^{+}}^{\mu}(L^{2}([0,1]))$. Here $\tilde{u}$ denotes
the extension of $u$ by zero to the whole $\mathbb{R}$. 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (v) Define the fractional Sobolev norm (cf.
\cite{DPV12})
\[
\|g\|_{W^{\mu,2}(\mathbb{R})}^{2}:=\|g\|^2_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}+\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|g_{t}-g_{s}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{1+2\mu}}dsdt,\quad g\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}).
\]
According to \cite[Proposition 3.4]{DPV12}, 
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|g_{t}-g_{s}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{1+2\mu}}dsdt=c_{\mu}\|[\omega\mapsto|\omega|^{\mu}\hat{g}(\omega)]\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}^{2}
\]
with some explicit constant $c_{\mu}.$ As a result, the $H^{\mu}$-
and $W^{\mu,2}$-norms are also equivalent. To complete the proof
of (\ref{eq:Equiv2}), it remains to show that 
\begin{equation}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\tilde{u}_{t}-\tilde{u}_{s}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{1+2\mu}}dsdt\leqslant C_{\mu}\Big[\|u\|_{L^{2}([0,1])}^{2}+\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{|u_{t}-u_{s}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{1+2\mu}}dsdt\Big]\label{eq:FracSobEst}
\end{equation}
for all $u\in I_{0^{+}}^{\mu}(L^{2}([0,1]))$.

To this end, one first writes 
\begin{align}
 & \int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\tilde{u}_{t}-\tilde{u}_{s}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{1+2\mu}}dsdt\nonumber \\
 & ={\cal I}(u)+2\int_{0}^{1}u_{t}^{2}\Big(\int_{-\infty}^{0}\frac{ds}{(t-s)^{1+2\mu}}+\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{ds}{(s-t)^{1+2\mu}}\Big)dt\Big)\nonumber \\
 & ={\cal I}(u)+\frac{1}{\mu}(A(u)+B(u)),\label{eq:FracSobDecomp}
\end{align}
where 
\[
{\cal I}(u):=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{|u_{t}-u_{s}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{1+2\mu}}dsdt,
\]
\[
A(u):=\int_{0}^{1}t^{-2\mu}u_{t}^{2}dt,\quad B(u):=\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)^{-2\mu}u_{t}^{2}dt.
\]
We only estimate $A(u)$. The integral $B(u)$ can be handled in the
same way by a change of variables $s=1-t.$

Let $\delta\in(0,1/3)$ and $\eta>0$. Define 
\[
A_{\delta}:=\int_{\delta}^{1}t^{-2\mu}u_{t}^{2}dt.
\]
It is obvious that 
\begin{equation}
\int_{1/3}^{1}t^{-2\mu}u_{t}^{2}dt\leqslant3^{2\mu}\|u\|_{2}^{2}.\label{eq:Third1Int}
\end{equation}
We now estimate the $\int_{\delta}^{1/3}$-integral. First of all,
one has the following elementary inequality 
\begin{equation}
u_{t}^{2}\leqslant(1+\eta)u_{s}^{2}+(1+\eta^{-1})(u_{t}-u_{s})^{2}\label{eq:EleIneq}
\end{equation}
for all $s,t$. By averaging (\ref{eq:EleIneq}) over $s\in(2t,3t)$
(i.e. applying $t^{-1}\int_{2t}^{3t}ds$ to both sides) and
then integrating against $t^{-2\mu}dt$ over $(\delta,1/3)$, one
finds that 
\begin{equation}
\int_{\delta}^{1/3}t^{-2\mu}u_{t}^{2}dt\leqslant(1+\eta)I_{\delta}+(1+\eta^{-1})J_{\delta},\label{eq:DelThirdInt}
\end{equation}
where 
\begin{align*}
I_{\delta} & :=\int_{\delta}^{1/3}t^{-1-2\mu}\int_{2t}^{3t}u_{s}^{2}dsdt,\\
J_{\delta} & :=\int_{\delta}^{1/3}t^{-1-2\mu}\int_{2t}^{3t}(u_{t}-u_{s})^{2}dsdt.
\end{align*}
By interchanging the iterated integrals, one has 
\begin{equation}
I_{\delta}  \leqslant\int_{2\delta}^{1}u_{s}^{2}\Big(\int_{s/3}^{s/2}t^{-1-2\mu}dt\Big)ds =a_{\mu}\int_{2\delta}^{1}s^{-2\mu}u_{s}^{2}ds\leqslant a_{\mu}A_{\delta},\label{eq:IDelEst}
\end{equation}
where 
\begin{equation}
a_{\mu}:=\int_{2}^{3}r^{2\mu-1}dr<1\label{eq:amu}
\end{equation}
and the last inequality follows from the fact that $(2\delta,1)\subseteq(\delta,1)$.
In addition, by using the inequality 
\[
t^{-1-2\mu}\leqslant\frac{2^{1+2\mu}}{(s-t)^{1+2\mu}}\quad\text{for all }s\in(2t,3t),
\]
one easily finds that 
\begin{equation}
J_{\delta}\leqslant2^{1+2\mu}{\cal I}(u).\label{eq:JDelEst}
\end{equation}
By substituting (\ref{eq:IDelEst}, \ref{eq:JDelEst}) into (\ref{eq:DelThirdInt})
and noting (\ref{eq:Third1Int}), it follows that 
\begin{equation}
A_{\delta}\leqslant(1+\eta)a_{\mu}A_{\delta}+(1+\eta^{-1})2^{1+2\mu}{\cal I}(u)+3^{2\mu}\|u\|_{2}^{2}.\label{eq:ADelIneq}
\end{equation}

Since $a_{\mu}<1$ (see (\ref{eq:amu})), one can fix a small $\eta$
so that $(1+\eta)a_{\mu}<1$. The estimate (\ref{eq:ADelIneq}) becomes
\[
A_{\delta}\leqslant\frac{1}{1-(1+\eta)a_{\mu}}\big((1+\eta^{-1})2^{1+2\mu}{\cal I}(u)+3^{2\mu}\|u\|_{2}^{2}\big).
\]
Note the the right hand side does not depend on $\delta.$ By taking
$\delta\downarrow0$, one concludes that 
\[
A(u)\leqslant C_{\mu}\big(\|u\|_{2}^{2}+{\cal I}(u)\big).
\]
The same estimate holds for $B(u)$. By applying these inequalities to
(\ref{eq:FracSobDecomp}), one obtains the desired estimate (\ref{eq:FracSobEst}).

Now the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:EquivNorm} is complete.

label: thm:RoughLowNC
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm:RoughLowNC}Let $X_{t}$ be the solution to the SDE (\ref{eq:SDEIntro}) with $H\in(1/4,1/2)$
and $V_{i}\in C_{b}^{\infty}$. Suppose that the vector fields $\{V_{1},\cdots,V_{d}\}$
satisfy Condition (NC). Then there exist positive constants $C_{1},C_{2}$
depending only on $H,V$ and dimensions, such that 
\[
\mathbb{P}(|X_{1}-x_{0}|>R)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2H+1}}
\]
for all large $R$.
head: environment

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
For the above theorem to hold, it is critical that $|I|\geqslant2$
in Condition (NC). The condition therefore captures the noncommutativity
of the vector fields $V_{1},\cdots,V_{d}$. If one allows $|I|=1$
(i.e., including the original vector fields $V_{i}$), one can at
best obtain a Gaussian lower bound 
\[
\mathbb{P}(|X_{1}-x_{0}|>R)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2}},
\]
which is consistent with the trivial example $(V_{1},\cdots,V_{d})={\rm id}$
($X_{t}=B_{t}$) (cf. Theorem \ref{thm:GenLowYoung}).
head: environment

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
A sufficient condition for (NC) is the following uniform nondegeneracy
condition on $V_{I}$.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (NC') There exist an integer $r\geqslant2$,
a positive constant $\kappa$ and a unit vector $\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$,
such that 
\[
\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}}\max_{I\in{\cal V}_{2}^{r}}\big|\langle V_{I}(x),\eta\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}\big|\geqslant\kappa.
\]
In fact, Condition (NC) follows by taking $F(x)=\langle\eta,x\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}.$

label: lem:LinDisplace
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem:LinDisplace}Under Condition (G), there exist constants
$\Lambda,\varepsilon_{0}$ $n_{0}$ depending only on $p,V,F,K,a$,
such that the following estimate 
\[
\big|X_{1}^{(n)}-x_{0}\big|\geqslant\Lambda n
\]
holds on the event $A_{n}(\varepsilon)$, uniformly for all $n>n_{0}$
and $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0}.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the previous construction and Property (G2), one has 
\[
F\Big(\Psi_{q_{k}^{(n)}}(X_{t_{k-1}}^{(n)})\Big)\geqslant F\big(X_{t_{k-1}}^{(n)}\big)+a
\]
for every $k$. On the other hand, since $F$ is globally Lipschitz
(say, with Lipschitz constant $C_{F}$) and $\|q_{k}^{(n)}\|_{1\text{-var}}\leqslant K$
by assumption, one knows from Lemma \ref{lem:LocCty} that 
\[
\Big|F\big(X_{t_{k}}^{(n)}\big)-F\Big(\Psi_{q_{k}^{(n)}}(X_{t_{k-1}}^{(n)})\Big)\Big|\leqslant C_{F}C_{p,V,K}\Big(\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};I_{k}}+\frac{1}{n}\Big),
\]
provided that $\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};I_{k}}\leqslant1.$ It follows
that 
\begin{align*}
F\big(X_{t_{k}}^{(n)}\big) & \geqslant F\big(X_{t_{k-1}}^{(n)}\big)+a-C_{p,V,K,F}\Big(\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};I_{k}}+\frac{1}{n}\Big),
\end{align*}
provided that $\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};I_{k}}\leqslant1.$ Now one
chooses
\[
\varepsilon_{0}\triangleq\frac{a}{4C_{p,V,K,F}}\wedge1,\quad n_{0}\triangleq\frac{4C_{p,V,K,F}}{a}.
\]
Then 
\[
F\big(X_{t_{k}}^{(n)}\big)\geqslant F\big(X_{t_{k-1}}^{(n)}\big)+\frac{a}{2}
\]
holds on the event $A_{n}(\varepsilon)$ uniformly for all $n>n_{0},$
$\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0}$ and $k=1,\cdots,n$. The conclusion
of the lemma thus follows by summing over $k$ and applying the global
Lipschitz property of $F$.

label: eq:InvKEst
title: Proof
body_md:
Now let $h^{(n)}$ be a given absolutely continuous path such that
$\|\dot{h}^{(n)}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leqslant Kn$ and $h_{t_{k-1}}^{^{(n)}}=h_{t_{k}}^{(n)}$
for every $k=1,\cdots,n.$ To prove the lemma, it suffices to show
that 
\begin{equation}
\big|\big(K_{H}^{-1}h^{(n)}\big)(t)\big|\leqslant C_{H}Kn^{H+1/2}\label{eq:InvKEst}
\end{equation}
for all $t\in[0,1]$. To this end, let $t\in I_{j}$ for some $j$.
We decompose the $s$-integral on the RHS of (\ref{eq:InvKForm})
into four parts:
\[
\int_{I_{1}}+\sum_{k=2}^{j-2}\int_{I_{k}}+\int_{I_{j-1}}+\int_{t_{j-1}}^{t}
\]
We estimate each part separately. 

Firstly, one has by assumption that
\begin{align*}
\Big|\int_{t_{j-1}}^{t}Q(t,s)\dot{h}_{s}^{(n)}ds\Big| & \leqslant C_{H}Kn\int_{t_{j-1}}^{t}(t-s)^{-(1/2+H)}(s/t)^{1/2-H}ds\\
 & \leqslant C_{H}Kn\int_{t_{j-1}}^{t}(t-s)^{-(1/2+H)}ds\\
 & \leqslant C_{H}Kn(t-t_{j-1})^{1/2-H}\leqslant C_{H}Kn^{H+1/2}.
\end{align*}
The integrals $\int_{I_{1}}$ and $\int_{I_{j-1}}$ are estimated
in the same way with the same $n^{H+1/2}$-growth. 

Next, consider the integral $\int_{I_{k}}$ with $2\leqslant k\leqslant j-2$.
Since $h_{t_{k-1}}^{(n)}=h_{t_{k}}^{(n)}$, one has 
\begin{align*}
&\Big|\int_{I_{k}}Q(t,s)\dot{h}_{s}^{(n)}ds\Big|\\
 & = \Big|\int_{I_{k}}\big(Q(t,s)-Q(t,t_{k})\big)\dot{h}_{s}^{(n)}ds\Big|\\
& \leqslant  C_{H}Kn\cdot\Big(\frac{j-1}{n}\Big)^{H-1/2}\cdot\Big[\Big(\frac{k-1}{n}\Big)^{-(1/2+H)}\Big(\frac{j-1-k}{n}\Big)^{-(1/2+H)}\\
 & \ \ \ +\Big(\frac{k}{n}\Big)^{1/2-H}\Big(\frac{j-1-k}{n}\Big)^{-(3/2+H)}\Big]\cdot\frac{1}{n^{2}},
\end{align*}
where the last inequality follows by estimating $\partial_{s}Q(t,s)$
in the obvious way. The exponent of $n$ on the RHS is precisely $H+1/2$.
It remains to see that 
\begin{equation}
(j-1)^{H-1/2}\sum_{k=2}^{j-2}(k-1)^{-(1/2+H)}(j-1-k)^{-(1/2+H)}\leqslant C_{H},\label{eq:kSumBound1}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
(j-1)^{H-1/2}\sum_{k=2}^{j-2}k^{1/2-H}(j-1-k)^{-(3/2+H)}\leqslant C_{H}\label{eq:kSumBound2}
\end{equation}
uniformly for all $j$. The inequality (\ref{eq:kSumBound1}) follows
by observing that the LHS is a Riemann sum approximation of the Beta
integral 
\[
\int_{0}^{1}x^{-(1/2+H)}(1-x)^{-(1/2+H)}dx.
\]
The inequality (\ref{eq:kSumBound1}) follows by observing that the
LHS is bounded above by 
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{j-2}(j-1-k)^{-(3/2+H)}\leqslant\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}l^{-(3/2+H)}=:C_{H}<\infty.
\]
Therefore, one concludes that 
\[
\Big|\sum_{k=2}^{j-2}\int_{I_{k}}Q(t,s)\dot{h}_{s}^{(n)}ds\Big|\leqslant C_{H}Kn^{H+1/2}.
\]

The desired claim (\ref{eq:InvKEst}) is easily obtained by combining
the above estimates. This completes the proof of the lemma.

label: lem:Fernique
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem:Fernique}There exist positive constants $C_{1},C_{2}$
depending only on $H,$ such that 
\[
\mathbb{P}(A_{n}(\varepsilon)^{c})\leqslant C_{1}ne^{-C_{2}\varepsilon^{2}n^{2H}}
\]
for all $n\geqslant1$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition, 
\[
\mathbb{P}(A_{n}(\varepsilon)^{c})=\mathbb{P}\big(\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};I_{k}}>\varepsilon\ \text{for some }k\big)\leqslant n\mathbb{P}\big(\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};[0,1]}>n^{H}\varepsilon\big),
\]
where we used a simple union bound and fBM scaling to reach the last
inequality. The result then follows from Fernique's estimate for Gaussian
rough paths (cf. \cite[Theorem 11.9]{FH14}).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $h^{(n)}\in\bar{{\cal H}}$ be constructed as before and set $\theta^{(n)}:=K_{H}^{-1}h^{(n)}$.
It is clear from construction that $\theta^{(n)}$ is ${\cal F}^{W}$-adapted,
where $W$ is the BM in the fBM representation. Consider the martingale
\[
M_{t}^{(n)}:=\int_{0}^{t}\langle\theta_{s}^{(n)},dW_{s}\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}.
\]
According to Corollary \ref{cor:CMEsthn}, one has 
\[
\langle M^{(n)}\rangle_{1}=\|\theta^{(n)}\|_{L^{2}([0,1])}^{2}\leqslant C_{H}^{2}K^{2}n^{2H+1}=:\Gamma_{n}
\]
for all $n$. 

Define the martingale 
\[
Z_{t}^{(n)}\triangleq\exp\Big(-\int_{0}^{t}\langle\theta_{s}^{(n)},dW_{s}\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\big|\theta_{s}^{(n)}\big|^{2}ds\Big),\quad0\leqslant t\leqslant1.
\]
According to Girsanov's theorem, under the new probability measure
$d\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}:=Z_{1}^{(n)}d\mathbb{P}$, the process 
\[
\tilde{W}_{t}^{(n)}:=W_{t}+\int_{0}^{t}\theta_{s}^{(n)}ds
\]
is a BM and hence $\tilde{B}_{t}^{(n)}:=B_{t}+h_{t}^{(n)}$ is an
fBM. Let $X_{t}$ be the solution to the SDE (\ref{eq:SDEIntro})
driven by ${\bf B}$ under $\mathbb{P}.$ Then one has
\begin{align*}
  \mathbb{P}\big(|X_{1}-x_{0}|\geqslant\Lambda n\big)
 & =\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}\big(\big|\Phi(1;0,x_{0},\tilde{B}^{(n)})-x_{0}\big|\geqslant\Lambda n\big)\\
 & =\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\big[Z_{1}^{(n)}{\bf 1}_{\{|\Phi(1;0,x_{0},\tilde{B}^{(n)})-x_{0}|\geqslant\Lambda n\}}\big]\\
 & \geqslant\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\big[Z_{1}^{(n)}{\bf 1}_{A_{n}(\varepsilon)}\big]
\end{align*}
for all $n>n_{0},$ $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0}$, where we used
Lemma \ref{lem:LinDisplace} to reach the last inequality with $\Lambda$
being the constant in that Lemma.

Now let 
\[
G_{n}\triangleq\big\{ M_{1}^{(n)}\leqslant\Gamma_{n}\big\}=\big\{ M_{1}^{(n)}\leqslant\Gamma_{n},\ \langle M^{(n)}\rangle_{1}\leqslant\Gamma_{n}\big\}.
\]
On the event $G_{n},$ one knows that $Z_{1}^{(n)}\geqslant e^{-3\Gamma_{n}/2}.$
In addition, by the exponential martingale inequality, one has 
\[
\mathbb{P}(G_{n}^{c})=\mathbb{P}\big(M_{1}^{(n)}>\Gamma_{n},\ \langle M^{(n)}\rangle_{1}\leqslant\Gamma_{n}\big)\leqslant2e^{-\Gamma_{n}/2}.
\]
It follows from Lemma \ref{lem:Fernique} that 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}\big(A_{n}(\varepsilon)\cap G_{n}\big) & =\mathbb{P}\big(A_{n}(\varepsilon)\big)-\mathbb{P}\big(A_{n}(\varepsilon)\cap G_{n}^{c}\big)\\
 & \geqslant1-C_{1}ne^{-C_{2}\varepsilon^{2}n^{2H}}-2e^{-\Gamma_{n}/2}.
\end{align*}
We fix $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0}.$ There exists $n_{1}>n_{0},$
such that 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(A_{n}(\varepsilon)\cap G_{n}\big)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}
\]
for all $n>n_{1}.$ As a consequence, one concludes that 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(|X_{1}-x_{0}|\geqslant\Lambda n\big)\geqslant\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\big[Z_{1}^{(n)}{\bf 1}_{A_{n}(\varepsilon)\cap G_{n}}\big]\geqslant\frac{1}{2}e^{-3\Gamma_{n}/2}=\frac{1}{2}e^{-3C_{H}^{2}K^{2}n^{2H+1}/2}
\]
for all $n>n_{1}$. 

The desired estimate (\ref{eq:RoughLowG}) follows by renaming $R:=\Lambda n$.

label: lem:CanPath
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem:CanPath}There exists a family $\{\gamma^{I}:I\in{\cal W}\}$
of piecewise linear paths such that the following properties hold
true:

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) $\pi^{(|I|)}S(\gamma^{I})={\bf 1}+e_{I}$
for every $I\in{\cal W}$;

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) for each $m\geqslant1$, there exists
a positive constant $L_{m}$ depending only on $m$, such that 
\[
\|\gamma^{I}\|_{1\text{-var}}\leqslant L_{m}
\]
for all $I\in{\cal W}$ with $|I|\leqslant m$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the lemma by induction on the length of the word. If $I=(i)$,
one simply defines $\gamma_{t}^{I}=te_{i}$ ($0\leqslant t\leqslant1$).
Suppose that $\gamma^{J}$ has been constructed to satisfy the required
properties for every word $J$ with $|J|<m$. Let $I$ be a word with
length $m$ and write $I=(i,J)$. One then defines 
\[
\gamma^{I}:=\gamma^{(i)}\sqcup\gamma^{J}\sqcup\overleftarrow{\gamma^{(i)}}\sqcup\overleftarrow{\gamma^{J}},
\]
where $\overleftarrow{\cdot}$ denotes the reversal of a path. By
the induction hypothesis, one can write 
\[
\pi^{(m)}\log S(\gamma^{J})=e_{J}+\xi
\]
where $\xi$ is some homogeneous Lie polynomial $\xi$ of degree $m$.
According to Chen's identity, one has
\begin{align*}
\pi^{(m)}\big[S(\gamma^{I})\big]= & \pi^{(m)}\big[\exp(e_{i})\otimes\exp(e_{J}+\xi)\otimes\exp(-e_{i})\otimes\exp(-e_{J}-\xi)\big]\\
= & \pi^{(m)}\Big[\Big(\sum_{p=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{p!}e_{i}^{\otimes p}\Big)\otimes\Big(\sum_{q=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{q!}(e_{J}+\xi)^{\otimes q}\Big)\otimes\Big(\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{r!}(-e_{i})^{\otimes r}\Big)\\
 & \ \ \ \otimes\Big(\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{s!}(-e_{J}-\xi)^{\otimes s}\Big)\Big].
\end{align*}
After expanding the above tensor products, it is plain algebra to
check that 
\[
\pi^{(m)}S(\gamma^{I})={\bf 1}+[e_{i},e_{J}]={\bf 1}+e_{I}.
\]
This proves Property (i) for $\gamma^{I}$. Property (ii) is obvious
because there are at most finitely many words of length $\leqslant m$.

label: lem:StocTaylor
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem:StocTaylor}Consider the following ODE:
\[
dy_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}V_{i}(y_{t})dq_{t}^{i},\quad y_{0}=x\in\mathbb{R}^{N},
\]
where $V_{1},\cdots,V_{d}$ are $C_{b}^{\infty}$-vector fields and
$q:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is a BV path. Then one has 
\begin{align*}
f(y_{1})= & f(x)+\sum_{k=1}^{r}\sum_{i_{1},\cdots,i_{k}=1}^{d}(V_{i_{1}}\cdots V_{i_{k}}f)(x)\int_{0<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{k}<1}dq_{t_{1}}^{i_{1}}\cdots dq_{t_{k}}^{i_{k}}\\
 & \ \ \ +\sum_{i_{1},\cdots,i_{r+1}=1}^{d}\int_{0<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{r+1}<1}(V_{i_{1}}\cdots V_{i_{r+1}}f)(y_{t_{1}})dq_{t_{1}}^{i_{1}}\cdots dq_{t_{r+1}}^{i_{r+1}}
\end{align*}
for any $r\geqslant1$ and any function $f:\mathbb{R}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$
that is continuously differentiable up to order $r+1.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is a simple consequence of iterative applications of the chain
rule.
head: environment

label: eq:FTay
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $r$ and $F$ be given by Condition (NC). According to Lemma \ref{lem:StocTaylor},
one has 
\begin{align}
F(\Psi_{q}(x))= & F(x)+\sum_{k=1}^{l}\sum_{i_{1},\cdots,i_{k}=1}^{d}(V_{i_{1}}\cdots V_{i_{k}}f)(x)\int_{0<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{k}<1}dq_{t_{1}}^{i_{1}}\cdots dq_{t_{k}}^{i_{k}}\nonumber \\
 & \ \ \ +R_{l+1}(x,q)\label{eq:FTay}
\end{align}
for all $l\leqslant r$, $x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ and BV paths $q:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d},$
where the remainder $R_{l+1}(x,q)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}}|R_{l+1}(x,q)|\leqslant C_{V,F,r}\|q\|_{1\text{-var }}^{l+1}\label{eq:TayRem}
\end{equation}
with some positive constant $C_{V,F,r}$ depending only on $r$, the
vector fields and $\|D^{l}F\|_{\infty}$ for $1\leqslant l\leqslant r+1$. 

Let ${\cal D}$ denote the space of smooth differential operators
over $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Let $\rho:T(\mathbb{R}^{d})\rightarrow{\cal D}$
be the algebra homomorphism induced by $\rho(e_{i}):=V_{i}$. The
expansion (\ref{eq:FTay}) can be rewritten as 
\begin{equation}
F(\Psi_{q}(x))=\big(\rho(\pi^{(l)}S(q))F\big)(x)+R_{l+1}(x,q).\label{eq:FTayAlg}
\end{equation}
In addition, one also notes that $\rho(e_{I})=V_{I}$ for any word
$I$. 

According to the assumption (\ref{eq:NC}), for each $x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$,
there exists a word $I(x)$ such that $2\leqslant|I(x)|\leqslant r$
and $|(V_{I(x)}F)(x)|\geqslant\kappa.$ Let 
\[
\sigma(x):={\rm sgn}\big[(V_{I(x)}F)(x)\big]
\]
so that 
\[
|(V_{I(x)}F)(x)|=\sigma(x)(V_{I(x)}F)(x)\geqslant\kappa.
\]
Given $\delta\in(0,1)$, we define for each $x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$
the absolutely continuous path 
\[
q_{x}^{\delta}:=(\delta\gamma^{I(x)})^{\sigma(x)}
\]
Here $\alpha{}^{-1}$ means the reversal of the path $\alpha$. One
knows from Lemma \ref{lem:CanPath} that 
\begin{equation}
\pi^{(|I(x)|)}S(q_{x}^{\delta})={\bf 1}+\delta^{|I(x)|}\sigma(x)e_{I(x)},\quad\|q_{x}^{\delta}\|_{1\text{-var}}\leqslant C_{r}\delta\label{eq:qxBd}
\end{equation}
for all $x$. 

It follows from the relation (\ref{eq:FTayAlg}) along with the properties
(\ref{eq:TayRem}, \ref{eq:qxBd}) that 
\[
\big|F\big(\Psi_{q_{x}^{\delta}}(x)\big)-F(x)-\delta^{|I(x)|}\sigma(x)(V_{I(x)}F)(x)\big|\leqslant C'_{V,F,r}\delta^{|I(x)|+1}.
\]
Therefore, 
\begin{align*}
F\big(\Psi_{q_{x}^{\delta}}(x)\big) & \geqslant F(x)+\delta^{|I(x)|}\sigma(x)(V_{I(x)}F)(x)-C'_{V,F,r}\delta^{|I(x)|+1}\\
 & \geqslant F(x)+\delta^{r}\big(\kappa-C'_{V,F,r}\delta\big).
\end{align*}
We choose $\delta:=\kappa/(2C'_{V,F,r})$ and define $a:=\kappa\delta^{r}/2$.
Then one has 
\[
F\big(\Psi_{q_{x}^{\delta}}(x)\big)\geqslant F(x)+a.
\]

To complete the proof, one simply chooses the same $F$ and takes
$q_{x}:=q_{x}^{\delta}$ (assuming that they are all parametrised
on $[0,1]$). Since $DF$ is bounded, $F$ is globally Lipschitz.
In addition, since $I(x)\geqslant2$ , one knows from the first relation
of (\ref{eq:qxBd}) that $q_{x}$ is a loop. It is also clear that
\[
K\triangleq\sup_{x}\|\dot{q}_{x}\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty,
\]
since the family $\{q_{x}\}$ only involves paths of the form $(\delta\gamma^{I})^{\pm1}$
($|I|\leqslant r$) whose totality is finite.

label: prop:BGNew
title: \protect\propositionname
body_md:

such that $\phi'(w_{0})\neq0$ at some $w_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$. Let
$B_{t}=(X_{t},Y_{t})$ be a two-dimensional fBM with Hurst parameter
$H\in(1/4,1/2).$ Then there exist positive constants $C_{1},C_{2}$,
such that the following estimate
\[
\mathbb{P}\Big(\Big|\int_{0}^{1}\phi(X_{t})dY_{t}\Big|\Big)>R\big)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2H+1}}
\]

head: environment

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:

slightly stronger and the authors only obtained a weaker estimate
with Weibull exponent being any $\gamma>2H+1$.
head: environment

label: eq:RDELineInt
title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the RDE 
\begin{equation}
dW_{t}=dX_{t},\ dZ_{t}=\phi(W_{t})dY_{t}\label{eq:RDELineInt}
\end{equation}
with $(W_{0},Z_{0})=(0,0).$ Then one has $Z_{1}=\int_{0}^{1}\phi(X_{t})dY_{t}$.
The underlying vector fields are given by $V_{1}=\partial_{w},$ $V_{2}=\phi(w)\partial_{z}$
and they satisfy $[V_{1},V_{2}]=\phi'(w)\partial_{z}$. Note that
the proposition is not an immediate consequence of Theorem \ref{thm:RoughLowNC},
since we do not impose a uniform nondegeneracy property on $\phi'$.
Instead, due to the rather special structure of the underlying RDE
(\ref{eq:RDELineInt}), the previous method can be easily adapted
to the current setting. We will only point out the essential changes. Without loss of generality, assume that $\phi'(w_0)>0$.

We consider the function $F(w,z):=z.$ Let $\kappa,\theta>0$ be such
that $\phi'(x)\geqslant\kappa$ for all $x\in[w_{0}-2\theta,w_{0}+2\theta]$.
Given $\delta>0$, consider the loop 
\[
q^{\delta}:=(\delta e_{w})\sqcup(\delta e_{z})\sqcup(-\delta e_{w})\sqcup(-\delta e_{z}),
\]
where $\{e_{w},e_{z}\}$ is the canonical basis of of the $(w,z)$-plane.
It is readily checked that 
\[
\Psi_{q^{\delta}}(w,z)=\big(w,z+\delta(\phi(w+\delta)-\phi(w))\big).
\]
In particular, 
\begin{align}
F\big(\Psi_{q^{\delta}}(w,z)\big)-F(w,z) & =\delta(\phi(w+\delta)-\phi(w))\nonumber \\
 & =\delta\int_{w}^{w+\delta}\phi'(u)du\geqslant\kappa\delta^{2}=:a\label{eq:Line1SDisp}
\end{align}
for any $w\in[w_{0}-\theta,w_{0}+\theta]$ and $\delta<\theta.$ This
essentially gives Condition (G) with the main difference being that
Condition (G2) only holds on the strip $\{(w,z):w\in[w_{0}-\theta,w_{0}+\theta]\}$. 

Let $n\geqslant1$. Construct the Cameron-Martin path 
\[
h^{(n)}:=\bar{q}\sqcup q_{1}^{(n)}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup q_{n}^{(n)}.
\]
Here $\bar{q}$ is the horizontal path from the origin to the point
$(w_{0},0)$ parametrised on $[0,1/2]$. The path $q_{k}^{(n)}$ is
$q^{\delta}$ reparametrised on $I_{k}:=[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{k-1}{2n},\frac{1}{2}+\frac{k}{2n}]$.
Let $U_{t}^{(n)}=(W_{t}^{(n)},Z_{t}^{(n)})$ ($0\leqslant t\leqslant1$)
be the solution to the RDE 
\[
\begin{cases}
dW_{t}^{(n)}=dX_{t}+dh_{t}^{(n),1}\\
dZ_{t}^{(n)}=\phi(W_{t}^{(n)})d\big(Y_{t}+h_{t}^{(n),2}\big)
\end{cases}
\]
with initial condition $(0,0)$. 

The key observation is that on the event $\{\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};[0,1]}\leqslant\theta\}$,
one has $W_{t_{k}}^{(n)}\in[w_{0}-\theta,w_{0}+\theta]$ for all $k=0,1,\cdots,n$.
Indeed, the construction of $h^{(n)}$ yields that 
\[
W_{t_{k}}^{(n)}=X_{t_{k}}+w_{0}
\]
for every $k$. As a result, 
\[
\big|W_{t_{k}}^{(n)}-w_{0}\big|=|X_{t_{k}}-0|\leqslant\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};[0,1]}\leqslant\theta.
\]
It follows from (\ref{eq:Line1SDisp}) that 
\[
F\big(\Psi_{q_{k}^{(n)}}(U_{t_{k-1}}^{(n)})\big)\geqslant F\big(U_{t_{k-1}}^{(n)}\big)+a
\]
for every $k$. 

One can now apply the same argument as in Section \ref{subsec:LinGrowth}
to conclude that 
\[
|U_{1}^{(n)}-U_{1/2}^{(n)}|\gtrsim n
\]
on the event 
\[
A_{n}'(\varepsilon):=\{\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};[0,1]}\}\bigcap\Big\{\max_{1\leqslant k\leqslant n}\|{\bf B}\|_{p\text{-var};I_{k}}\leqslant\varepsilon\Big\}.
\]
In addition, since each $q_{k}^{(n)}$ is a loop, one can argue in
the same way as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:CMEst} to show that
\[
\|h^{(n)}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}\lesssim n^{H+1/2}
\]
for all $n$ (the additional part $\bar{q}$ only produces a bounded
contribution). The desired lower tail estimate is then established
by applying the same Girsanov-type argument as before.

label: eq:RightInv
title: Proof
body_md:
The argument is identical to the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:RoughLowG}. The main observation is that Condition (G) in Section \ref{sec:CondG} remains valid but without requiring $q_x$ to be a loop in (G1). Indeed, let $\eta$ be a fixed unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^N$ and define $F(x):=\langle x,\eta\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^N}$. Let 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:RightInv}
A(x):=V(x)^T\big(V(x)V(x)^T\big)^{-1}
\end{equation}be the right inverse of $V=(V_1,\cdots,V_d)$, which is well-defined due to ellipticity. Given $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$, the control  
\[
q_x(t):=\int_0^t A(x+s\eta)\eta ds
\]satisfies $\|\dot{q_x}\|_{\infty}\leqslant \|A\|_\infty$ and $F(\Psi_{q_x}(x)) = F(x) + 1$. Therefore, Condition (G) without the loop requirement in (G1) holds with $K = \|A\|_\infty$ and $a=1$.

The only change to the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:RoughLowG} is that the Cameron-Martin estimate (\ref{eq:CmEstRoughLow}) becomes 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:CMEstUE}
\|h^{(n)}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}\leqslant C_{H}Kn.
\end{equation}The estimate (\ref{eq:CMEstUE}) follows directly from the elementary inequality $\|h\|_{\bar{\cal H}}\leqslant C_H \|\dot{h}\|_\infty$, which can be seen by using the same representation (\ref{eq:InvKForm}). With the change of exponent from $H+1/2$ to $1$, one can now carry through exactly the same argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:RoughLowG} to deduce the desired Gaussian lower bound (\ref{eq:GenLowRough}).

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md: It is clear from the above argument that the upgrade of a Gaussian lower tail to $(2H+1)$-Weibull is precisely due to the additional loop property in Condition (G1). From a geometric viewpoint, the possibility of moving the dynamics around by using \textit{loop} controls is a consequence of the noncommutativity of the vector fields (Condition (NC)).

label: eq:LamNorm
title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the linear functional 
\[
\Lambda:\bar{{\cal H}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\quad\Lambda(h):=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\varepsilon_{k}}{l_{k}}\big(h_{t_{k}}-h_{s_{k}}\big).
\]
We claim that 
\begin{equation}
\|\Lambda\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}^{*}}^{2}={\rm Var}\Big[\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\varepsilon_{k}}{l_{k}}(B_{t_{k}}-B_{s_{k}})\Big].\label{eq:LamNorm}
\end{equation}
Indeed, under the canonical isometric isomorphisms $\bar{{\cal H}}^{*}\cong\bar{{\cal H}}\cong\mathcal{C}_{1}^{B}$
(the last denotes the first Wiener chaos of $B$), the chaos element
corresponding to the functional $[h\mapsto h_{t}]$ is $B_{t}$ for
every given $t$. By linearity, the chaos element corresponding to
$\Lambda$ is 
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\varepsilon_{k}}{l_{k}}(B_{t_{k}}-B_{s_{k}}).
\]
This proves the claim (\ref{eq:LamNorm}). On the other hand, for
any $h\in\bar{{\cal H}}$ satisfying the assumption of the lemma,
one has 
\[
\Lambda(h)\geqslant a\sum_{k=1}^{n}l_{k}^{-1}.
\]
The desired estimate (\ref{eq:CMLowVar}) follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz
inequality and the relation (\ref{eq:LamNorm}).

label: lem:fFId
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem:fFId} Let $\beta\in(0,1)$. Then one has 
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}f(u)f(v)|u-v|^{-\beta}dudv=\beta(1+\beta)\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\|\Delta_{r}F\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}^{2}}{r^{2+\beta}}dr
\]
for all bounded and compactly supported $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$,
where $F(x):=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(u)du$ and $(\Delta_{r}F)(x):=F(x+r)-F(x)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition, one has 
\begin{align*}
\|\Delta_{r}F\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}^{2} & =\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\Big(\int_{x}^{x+r}f(u)du\Big)\Big(\int_{x}^{x+r}f(v)dv\Big)dx\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}f(u)f(v)\Big[\int_{\mathbb{R}}{\bf 1}_{[u-r,u]\cap[v-r,v]}(x)dx\Big]dudv\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}f(u)f(v)\big(r-|u-v|\big)_{+}dudv.
\end{align*}
It follows that 
\[
\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\|\Delta_{r}F\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}^{2}}{r^{2+\beta}}dr=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}f(u)f(v)\Big[\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\big(r-|u-v|\big)_{+}}{r^{2+\beta}}dr\Big]dudv.
\]
The $dr$-integral is easily evaluated as 
\[
\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\big(r-|u-v|\big)_{+}}{r^{2+\beta}}dr=\frac{|u-v|^{-\beta}}{\beta(1+\beta)}.
\]
The desired relation thus follows.

only on $H$, such that

title: Proof
body_md:
According to Lemma \ref{lem:CMLowVar} and Lemma \ref{lem:VarEst},
one has 
\[
\|h\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}^{2}\geqslant C_{H}a^{2}\cdot\frac{\big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}l_{k}^{-1}\big)^{2}}{\big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}l_{k}^{-(2-2H)}\big).}
\]
Denote $x_{k}:=l_{k}^{-1}$ and $\beta:=2-2H$. Since $\beta\in(0,1)$,
concavity of $x\mapsto x^{\beta}$ implies that 
\[
\frac{\big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}\big)^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}^{\beta}}=\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}\Big)^{2-\beta}\frac{\big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}\big)^{\beta}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}^{\beta}}\geqslant n^{\beta-1}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}\Big)^{2-\beta}.
\]
On the other hand, since 
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}^{-1}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}l_{k}\leqslant1,
\]
the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality shows that 
\[
n^{2}\leqslant\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}^{-1}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}\Big)\leqslant\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}.
\]
As a consequence, 
\[
\|h\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}^{2}\geqslant C_{H}a^{2}\cdot n^{\beta-1}\cdot n^{2(2-\beta)}=C_{H}a^{2}n^{2H+1}.
\]
This completes the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:CMLowFluct}.

label: prop:GauIso
title: \protect\propositionname
body_md:
\label{prop:GauIso}Let $Z$ be a centered, nondegenerate Gaussian
vector. Let $K$ be a closed, convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
Suppose that 
\[
r:=d_{{\cal H}_{Z}}(o,K):=\inf_{z\in K}\|z\|_{{\cal H}_{Z}}>0.
\]
Then 
\[
\mathbb{P}(Z\in K)\leqslant1-\Phi(r),
\]
where $\Phi(t):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-u^{2}/2}du$
is the standard normal distribution function.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is essentially the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality (cf. \cite{Led94}).
For completeness, let us provide the short and simple proof in the
current finite dimensional setting. Let $Q:={\rm Cov}[Z]$ and define
$X:=Q^{-1/2}Z\sim N(0,{\rm Id})$. Also set $L:=Q^{-1/2}K$. Note
that $L$ is again a closed, convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. In
addition, one has 
\[
d_{\,\mathbb{R}^{n}}(o,L)=\inf_{x\in L}|x|_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}=\inf_{z\in K}\big|Q^{-1/2}z\big|_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}=\inf_{z\in K}\|z\|_{{\cal H}_{Z}}=r.
\]
Let $x_{*}\in L$ be the unique minimiser of $L\ni x\mapsto|x|_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}$.
Convexity implies that 
\[
\langle x_*,x-x_{*}\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\geqslant0
\]
for all $x\in L$. As a result, one has 
\[
L\subseteq\big\{ x:\langle u,x\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\geqslant r\big\},
\]
where $u:=x_{*}/|x_{*}|_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}$. It follows that 
\[
\mathbb{P}(Z\in K)=\mathbb{P}(X\in L)\leqslant\mathbb{P}\big(\langle u,X\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\geqslant r\big)=1-\Phi(r),
\]
since $\langle u,X\rangle\sim N(0,1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the nondegenerate Gaussian vector 
\[
Z:=\Big(\varepsilon_{k}(B_{t_{k}}-B_{s_{k}})\Big)_{k=1}^{n}.
\]
Define the projection 
\[
P_{Z}:\bar{{\cal H}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n},\quad P_{Z}(h):=\Big(\varepsilon_{k}(h_{t_{k}}-h_{s_{k}})\Big)_{k=1}^{n}.
\]
It is standard that ${\cal H}_{Z}=P_{Z}(\bar{{\cal H}})=\mathbb{R}^{n}$
and 
\begin{equation}
|z|_{{\cal H}_{Z}}=\inf\big\{\|h\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}:P_{Z}(h)=z\big\}.\label{eq:CMProj}
\end{equation}
Let $K:=[a,\infty)^{n}.$ According to Lemma \ref{lem:CMLowFluct}
and (\ref{eq:CMProj}), one has 
\[
d_{{\cal H}_{Z}}(o,K)\geqslant C_{H}an^{H+1/2},
\]
where $C_{H}$ is a positive constant that does not depend on $a,n$
or the grid points $s_{i},t_{j}$. It follows from Proposition \ref{prop:GauIso}
that 
\[
\mathbb{P}(Z\in K)\leqslant2e^{-C_{H}'a^{2}n^{2H+1}}.
\]
This yields the desired inequality (\ref{eq:FixGdEst}).

label: lem:GenProbEst
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem:GenProbEst}There exist positive constants $C_{1},C_{2}$
depending only on $H$ and an integer $N$ depending only on $H,a$$,$
such that the estimate 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(\big\{ E_{{\bf s},{\bf t}}(a)\ \text{occurs for some }\text{partition}({\bf s},{\bf t})\in{\cal P}_{n}\big\}\big)\leqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}a^{2}n^{2H+1}}
\]
holds for all $n>N$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define 
\[
E_{n}(a):=\big\{ E_{{\bf s},{\bf t}}(a)\ \text{occurs for some }\text{partition }({\bf s},{\bf t})\in{\cal P}_{n}\big\}.
\]
Let $\delta_{n}:=n^{-q}$ with $q$ being specified later on. Let
${\cal D}(\delta_{n})$ be the partition of $[0,1]$ into equal subintervals
of length $\delta_{n}$. Consider the event 
\[
G_{n}(a):=\Big\{ m_{B}(2\delta_{n})<\frac{a}{4}\Big\},
\]
where 
\[
m_{B}(\delta):=\sup_{s,t\in[0,1],|t-s|\leqslant\delta}|B_{t}-B_{s}|
\]
is the modulus of continuity of $B$. 

We claim that 
\[
E_{n}(a)\cap G_{n}(a)\subseteq\bigcup_{\substack{(\hat{{\bf s}},\hat{{\bf t}})\in{\cal P}_{n}\\
\hat{s}_{i},\hat{t}_{j}\in{\cal D}(\delta_{n})
}
}E_{\hat{{\bf s}},\hat{{\bf t}}}(a/2).
\]
Indeed, let $\omega\in{\rm LHS}$. Then 
\begin{equation}
\varepsilon_{k}\big(B_{t_{k}}-B_{s_{k}}\big)\geqslant a\label{eq:OsIncfBM}
\end{equation}
holds with some $2n$-tuple $({\bf s},{\bf t})$ for every $k$. It
is obvious that $t_{k}-s_{k}>2\delta_{n}$ for every $k$, for otherwise
the relation (\ref{eq:OsIncfBM}) would contradict the fact that $m_{\omega}(2\delta_{n})<a/4$.
Define the $2n$-tuple $(\hat{{\bf s}},\hat{{\bf t}})$ where $\hat{s}_{k}>s_{k}$
(respectively, $\hat{t}_{k}<t_{k}$) is the partition point in ${\cal D}(\delta_{n})$
that is closest to $s_{k}$ from the right (respectively, closest
to $t_{k}$ from the left). The points $\hat{s}_{k},\hat{t}_{k}$
exist because $t_{k}-s_{k}>2\delta_{n}$. It follows that 
\begin{align*}
\varepsilon_{k}\big(B_{\hat{t}_{k}}-B_{\hat{s}_{k}}\big) & \geqslant\varepsilon_{k}\big(B_{t_{k}}-B_{t_{k}}\big)-\big|B_{s_{k}}-B_{\hat{s}_{k}}\big|-\big|B_{t_{k}}-B_{\hat{t}_{k}}\big|\\
 & \geqslant a-2\omega_{B}(\delta_{n})>a-\frac{a}{2}=\frac{a}{2}
\end{align*}
for every $k$. This proves the claim. 

Note that the cardinality of $2n$-tuples $(\hat{{\bf s}},\hat{{\bf t}})$
chosen from the partition ${\cal D}(\delta_{n})$ is at most 
\[
|{\cal D}(\delta_{n})|^{2n}=e^{2nq\log n}.
\]
According to Lemma \ref{lem:FixGdEst}, one obtains that 
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}\big(E_{n}(a)\cap G_{n}(a)\big)\leqslant e^{2nq\log n}\times C_{1}e^{-C_{2}a^{2}n^{2H+1}}.\label{eq:EnaMain}
\end{equation}
The first term is negligible comparing to the second term for all
$n>N(H,a,q).$

Now it remains to estimate $\mathbb{P}(G_{n}(a)^{c}).$ To this end,
we first claim that 
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}(m_{B}(r)>\lambda)\leqslant c_H r^{-1}e^{-C_{H}\lambda^{2}/r^{2H}}\label{eq:TailMod}
\end{equation}
for all $r\in(0,1)$ and $\lambda>0$. Indeed, note that 
\[
m_{B}(r)\leqslant2\max_{0\leqslant k\leqslant r^{-1}-2}\sup_{t\in J_{k}}\big|B_{t}-B_{kr}\big|
\]
where $J_{k}:=[kr,(k+2)r].$ By applying a simple union bound, the
fractional Brownian scaling and Borel's inequality (see \cite[Theorem 2.1]{Adl90}),
one finds that 
\[
\mathbb{P}(m_{B}(r)>\lambda)\leqslant  r^{-1}\mathbb{P}\Big(\sup_{t\in[0,2]}|\tilde{B}_{t}|>\frac{u}{2r^{H}}\Big)\leqslant c_H r^{-1}e^{-C_{H}u^{2}/r^{2H}}.
\]
This proves the estimate (\ref{eq:TailMod}). It follows that 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(G_{n}(a)^{c}\big)\leqslant C_{3}n^{q}e^{-C_{4}a^{2}n^{2Hq}}.
\]
By choosing $q>1+\frac{1}{2H}$, the RHS of the above inequality is
negligible comparing to the main estimate (\ref{eq:EnaMain}). As
a consequence, one concludes that 
\[
\mathbb{P}(E_{n}(a))\leqslant\mathbb{P}\big(E_{n}(a)\cap G_{n}(a)\big)+\mathbb{P}(G_{n}(a)^{c})\leqslant C_{5}e^{-C_{6}a^{2}n^{2H+1}}
\]
for all $n>N(H,a)$.

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
Let $h:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$ be an absolutely continuous
path. Let $\mu_{h}(dt):=|\dot{h}_{t}|dt$ denote its arclength measure.
An interval $I=[u,v]\subseteq[0,1]$ is said to \textit{contain an
$(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective turn} of $h$ if there are measurable
subsets $A,B\subseteq I$ such that 
\[
\mu_{h}(A)\geqslant a_{0},\quad\mu_{h}(B)\geqslant a_{0}
\]
and 
\[
\text{\ensuremath{\angle}\ensuremath{\Big(}\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\frac{\dot{h}_{s}}{|\dot{h}_{s}|}}},\ensuremath{\frac{\dot{h}_{t}}{|\dot{h}_{t}|}}\Big)\ensuremath{\geqslant}\ensuremath{\theta_{0}}}
\]
for $\mu_{h}\otimes\mu_{h}$-a.e. $(s,t)\in A\times B$ at which $\dot{h}_{s}\neq0$
and $\dot{h}_{t}\neq0$. We define ${\cal N}_{{\rm eff}}(h)$ to be
the maximal number of disjoint intervals in $[0,1]$ that contain
an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective turn of $h$.
head: environment

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
Heuristically, an effective turn consists of two pieces of $h$ on
$I$ which have arclength at least $a_{0}$ and have angle separately
uniformly by at least $\theta_{0}.$

\label{lem:CMEffTurn}There exists a positive constant $C_{H}$ depending
only on $H$, such that 
\[
\|h\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}\geqslant C_{H}a_{0}\sin\Big(\frac{\theta_{0}}{2}\Big)\cdot{\cal N}_{{\rm eff}}(h)^{H+1/2}
\]
for all $h\in\bar{{\cal H}}$.

label: eq:HeavClose
title: Proof
body_md:
This is a simple consequence of the definition of effective turn.
Let $w_{k}$ be the center of $P_{k}$ for every $k$. We claim that
\begin{equation}
\angle(w_{k},w_{l})\leqslant\theta_{0}+\frac{2\pi}{m_{0}}\label{eq:HeavClose}
\end{equation}
for any pair $P_{k},P_{l}$ of heavy arcs. Indeed, suppose that (\ref{eq:HeavClose})
is not true for some heavy pair $P_{k},P_{l}$. Let 
\[
A:=\Big\{ t\in I:\dot{h}_{t}\neq0,\ \frac{\dot{h}_{t}}{|\dot{h}_{t}|}\in P_{k}\Big\},\quad B:=\Big\{ t\in I:\dot{h}_{t}\neq0,\ \frac{\dot{h}_{t}}{|\dot{h}_{t}|}\in P_{l}\Big\}.
\]
Then one has
\begin{align*}
\ensuremath{\angle}\Big(\ensuremath{\frac{\dot{h}_{s}}{|\dot{h}_{s}|}},\ensuremath{\frac{\dot{h}_{t}}{|\dot{h}_{t}|}}\Big) & \geqslant\angle(w_{k},w_{l})-\ensuremath{\angle}\Big(\ensuremath{\frac{\dot{h}_{s}}{|\dot{h}_{s}|}},\ensuremath{\frac{\dot{h}_{t}}{|\dot{h}_{t}|}}\Big)\\
 & >\theta_{0}+\frac{2\pi}{m_{0}}-\frac{2\pi}{m_{0}}=\theta_{0}
\end{align*}
for $\mu_{h}\otimes\mu_{h}$-a.e. $(s,t)\in A\times B$. Since $P_{k},P_{l}$
are heavy, it follows that $(A,B)$ provides an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective
turn of $h$ in $I$. This is a contradiction. Therefore, the estimate
(\ref{eq:HeavClose}) holds.

Now let $v_{*}$ be the center of a given heavy arc (which exists
by assumption). Define 
\[
E:=\Big\{ t\in I:\dot{h}_{t}\neq0,\ \frac{\dot{h}_{t}}{|\dot{h}_{t}|}\in P_{{\rm light}}\Big\},
\]
where $P_{{\rm light}}$ denotes the union of all light arcs. Since
there are at most $m_{0}$ light arcs, one has by definition that
$\mu_{h}(E)\leqslant m_{0}a_{0}.$ This proves the first claim (\ref{eq:LightLength}).
In addition, according to the estimate (\ref{eq:HeavClose}), all
heavy arcs lie inside the cone centered at $v_{*}$ with $S^{1}$-radius
\[
\theta_{0}+\frac{2\pi}{m_{0}}+2\times\frac{\pi}{m_{0}}=\theta_{0}+\frac{4\pi}{m_{0}}.
\]
This proves the second claim (\ref{eq:HeavyConcen}).

label: lem:ILength
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem:ILength}Let $I=[u,v]\subseteq[0,1]$ and $a>2$. Suppose
that $I$ does not contain an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective turn
of $h$. Suppose further that 
\[
r_{u}=a,\quad r_{v}=a+3\pi
\]
and $r_{t}\in[a,a+3\pi]$ for all $t\in I$. Then $\mu_{h}(I)\geqslant\gamma_{0}a.$
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $R>4$. Let $h\in\bar{{\cal H}}$ be such that $r_{t}:=|X_{t}^{h}|\geqslant R$
for some $t\in[0,1]$. We decompose the annulus $\{x:R/2\leqslant|x|\leqslant R\}$
into disjoint concentric annuli
\[
A_{j}:=\{x:a_{j}\leqslant|x|\leqslant b_{j}\},\quad a_{j}:=\frac{R}{2}+3\pi(j-1),b_{j}:=a_{j}+3\pi.
\]
There are $N_{R}=\frac{R}{6\pi}$ of them. Using first and last hitting,
one can find a sequence of times 
\[
0<s_{1}<t_{1}<\cdots<s_{N_{R}}<t_{N_{R}}<1,
\]
such that $r_{s_{j}}=a_{j},r_{t_{j}}=b_{j}$ and $r_{t}\in[a_{j},b_{j}]$
for every $j$. Let $I_{j}:=[s_{j},t_{j}]$. Denote 
\[
{\cal B}:=\{j:I_{j}\text{ does not contain an }(a_{0},\theta_{0})\text{-effective turn of }h\}.
\]
According to Lemma \ref{lem:ILength}, one has 
\[
\mu_{h}(I_{j})\geqslant\gamma_{0}a_{j}\geqslant\frac{\gamma_{0}R}{2}
\]
for every $j\in{\cal B}$. It follows that 
\[
\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}\geqslant\sum_{j\in{\cal B}}\mu_{h}(I_{j})\geqslant\frac{\gamma_{0}R}{2}\cdot|{\cal B}|.
\]
Therefore, 
\[
|{\cal B}|\leqslant\frac{2\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}}{\gamma_{0}R}.
\]
The number of $j$'s such that $I_{j}$ contains an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective
turn is thus bounded below by 
\[
N_{R}-|{\cal B}|\geqslant\frac{R}{6\pi}-\frac{2\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}}{\gamma_{0}R}.
\]
The desired estimate (\ref{eq:NonPertCoer}) now follows from the
definition of ${\cal N}_{{\rm eff}}(h).$

label: lem:TurnEstPert
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem:TurnEstPert}There exist positive constants $C_{1},C_{2},R_{0}$
depending only on $p,\theta,V$, such that the estimate
\begin{equation}
{\cal N}_{{\rm eff}}(h)\geqslant C_{1}R-C_{2}\Big[M^{p}+M^{1+\theta}+MR^{1-1/p}+\frac{\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}}{R}+M\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}^{\theta}\Big]\label{eq:TurnEstPert}
\end{equation}
holds uniformly over all $R>R_{0}$, all $h\in\bar{{\cal H}}$ and
all $w\in C^{p\text{-var}}([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{2})$ satisfying
\[
\sup_{0\leqslant t\leqslant1}|X_{t}^{w+h}|\geqslant R
\]
and $\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $R>R_{0}$ and let $(w,h)\in C^{p\text{-var}}([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{2})\times\bar{{\cal H}}$
be given such that 
\[
\sup_{0\leqslant t\leqslant1}|X_{t}^{w+h}|\geqslant R,\quad\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M.
\]
If $\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}>R^{H+1/2},$ one can use the simple inequality
(cf. (\ref{eq:EquivFracNorm}))
\[
\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}\leqslant C_{H}\|h\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}
\]
to deduce that 
\[
\|h\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}\geqslant C_{H}^{-1}R^{H+1/2}.
\]
Now consider the case when $\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}\leqslant R^{H+1/2}$.
According to Lemma \ref{lem:CMEffTurn} and Lemma \ref{lem:TurnEstPert},
\begin{align*}
\|h\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}\geqslant & C_{H}\Big[C_{1}R-C_{2}\Big(M^{p}+M^{1+\theta}+MR^{1-1/p}\\
 & \ \ \ +R^{H-1/2}+MR^{\theta(H+1/2)}\Big)\Big]^{H+1/2}.
\end{align*}
Since $\theta(H+1/2)<1$, one has 
\[
C_{2}\Big(M^{p}+M^{1+\theta}+MR^{1-1/p}+R^{H-1/2}+MR^{\theta(H+1/2)}\Big)\leqslant\frac{C_{1}R}{2}
\]
whenever $R>R_{*}$ for some constant $R_{*}$ depending additionally
on $M$. It follows that 
\[
\|h\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}\geqslant c_{*}R^{H+1/2}
\]
with a suitable constant $c_{*}>0$ for all $R>R_{M}.$

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
It is clear from the above proof that the constant $c_{*}$ does not
depend on $M$.

label: eq:pVarEstPf
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $I=[u,v]$. One has 
\[
X_{s,t}=\int_{s}^{t}V(X_{r})dw_{r}+\int_{s}^{t}V(X_{r})dh_{r}
\]
for all $s\leqslant t\in I.$ The $dh$-integral is easily estimated
as 
\[
\Big\|\int_{u}^{\cdot}V(X_{t})dh_{t}\Big\|_{p\text{-var};I}\leqslant\|V\|_{\infty}l_{I}.
\]
For the $dw$-integral, one has from \cite[Theorem 6.8]{FV10} (Young's
integral estimate) that 
\[
\Big\|\int_{u}^{\cdot}V(X_{r})dw_{r}\Big\|_{p\text{-var};I}\leqslant C_{p}\big(\|V\|_{\infty}+\|DV\|_{\infty}\omega_{I}\big)\omega_{I}.
\]
Therefore, 
\begin{align}
\|X\|_{p\text{-var};I} & \leqslant\|V\|_{\infty}l_{I}+C_{p}\big(\|V\|_{\infty}+\|DV\|_{\infty}\|X\|_{p\text{-var};I}\big)\omega_{I}\nonumber \\
 & \leqslant C_{1;p,V}(l_{I}+\omega_{I})+C_{2;p,V}\omega_{I}\|X\|_{p\text{-var};I}.\label{eq:pVarEstPf}
\end{align}
Choose $\delta$ to be such that 
\[
C_{2;p,V}\delta\leqslant\frac{1}{2}.
\]
It follows from (\ref{eq:pVarEstPf}) that 
\[
\|X\|_{p\text{-var};I}\leqslant C_{1;p,V}(l_{I}+\omega_{I})+\frac{1}{2}\|X\|_{p\text{-var};I}\iff\|X\|_{p\text{-var};I}\leqslant2C_{1;p,V}(l_{I}+\omega_{I}),
\]
provided that $\omega_{I}\leqslant\delta$. This yields the desired
estimate (\ref{eq:WHCty}).

\Xi_{I}:=\omega_{I}\big(1+(\omega_{I}+l_{I})^{\theta}\big)

for each $I=[u,v]\subseteq[0,1]$. There exists a positive constant

and $w\in C^{p\text{-var}}([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{2})$ satisfying
$\omega_{I}\leqslant\delta$ and $r_{t}\geqslant a$ for all $t\in I$.

label: eq:Eta01
title: Proof
body_md:
By choosing $\eta_{0}$ small, one can always ensure that there is
at least a heavy arc with respect to $h|_{I}$. Indeed, since $\|A\|_{\infty}=1$,
one finds from the equation (\ref{eq:RPertEqn}) of $r_{t}$ that
\[
3\pi=r_{v}-r_{u}\leqslant K\Xi_{I}+l_{I}\leqslant K\eta_{0}+l_{I},
\]
provided that $\Xi_{I}\leqslant\eta_{0}.$ Suppose that 
\begin{equation}
\eta_{0}<\frac{1}{K}(3\pi-m_{0}a_{0})=\frac{23\pi}{8K}.\label{eq:Eta01}
\end{equation}
Then one has 
\[
l_{I}\geqslant3\pi-K\eta_{0}>m_{0}a_{0}.
\]
This implies by definition that there must be at least one heavy arc
(otherwise, $l_{I}\leqslant m_{0}a_{0}$).

Now suppose that the conditions (\ref{eq:WHAs1}, \ref{eq:WHAs2},
\ref{eq:WHAs3}) are all satisfied while $I$ does not contain an
$(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective turn of $h$. We will show that this
leads to a contradiction if $A_{0}$ and $\eta_{0}$ are chosen properly.
First of all, by using the given conditions, the $\phi$-equation
(\ref{eq:PhiPertEqn}) and Corollary \ref{cor:YoungPertEst}, one
finds that 
\[
\sup_{s,t\in I}|\phi_{t}-\phi_{s}|\leqslant\frac{K}{a}\Xi_{I}+\frac{1}{a}\mu_{h}(I)\leqslant\frac{K\eta_{0}}{A_{0}}+\frac{\gamma_{0}}{2}.
\]
By requiring that 
\begin{equation}
\frac{K\eta_{0}}{A_{0}}<\frac{\gamma_{0}}{2},\label{eq:A0}
\end{equation}
one has 
\[
\sup_{s,t\in I}|\phi_{t}-\phi_{s}|<\gamma_{0}.
\]
In addition, according to Lemma \ref{lem:HeavyConcen}, there exist
a measurable subset $E\subseteq I$ and a unit vector $v_{*}=e^{i\alpha_{*}}$
such that (\ref{eq:LightLength}) and (\ref{eq:HeavyConcen}) holds.
One can then carry the argument of Lemma \ref{lem:ILength} word by
word to show that 
\begin{equation}
{\rm dist}_{2\pi}(r_{t}+\alpha_{t}-\phi_{t},\pi)\leqslant\frac{\pi}{2}\label{eq:NegCosPertPf}
\end{equation}
for $\mu_{h}$-a.e. $t\in I\backslash E$ such that $\dot{h}_{t}\neq0$
and $r_{t}\in[\beta_{*}-m_{0}a_{0},\beta_{*}+m_{0}a_{0}]$, where
$\beta_{*}$ is defined according to the relation (\ref{eq:Beta*}).
Define $t_{\pm}$ as in (\ref{eq:tpm}). It follows from the $r$-equation
(\ref{eq:RPertEqn}), Corollary \ref{cor:YoungPertEst}, the estimates
(\ref{eq:LightLength}) and (\ref{eq:NegCosPertPf}) that 

\begin{align*}
2m_{0}a_{0} & =r_{t_{+}}-r_{t_{-}}=\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}dr_{s}\\
 & =\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}A(X_{s})dw_{s}+\int_{t_{-}}^{t_{+}}\cos(r_{s}+\alpha_{s}-\phi_{s})|\dot{h}_{s}|ds\\
 & \leqslant K\Xi_{I}+\mu_{h}(E)\leqslant K\eta_{0}+m_{0}a_{0}.
\end{align*}
By requiring $\eta_0$ to satisfy
\begin{equation}
K\eta_{0}<m_{0}a_{0},\label{eq:Eta02}
\end{equation}
one reaches a contradiction. 

To summarise, one first chooses $\eta_{0}$ that satisfies (\ref{eq:Eta01},
\ref{eq:Eta02}) and then chooses $A_{0}$ to satisfy (\ref{eq:A0}).
With such choices, for any $(I,a;w,h)$ satisfying the conditions
(\ref{eq:WHAs1}, \ref{eq:WHAs2}, \ref{eq:WHAs3}), the interval
$I$ must contain an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective turn of $h$.
This completes the proof of the lemma.

title: Proof
body_md:
We continue to use the same notation as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:NonPertCoer}
(the annuli decomposition $[a_{j},b_{j}]$ and radial crossing $I_{j}=[s_{j},t_{j}]$).
Let $R>2A_{0}$ ($A_{0}$ is the constant appearing in Lemma \ref{lem:ILengthPert}
so that $a_{j}>A_{0}$ for every $j$). Our goal is to estimate the
number of $I_{j}$'s which do not contain an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective
turn of $h$. According to Lemma \ref{lem:ILengthPert}, at least
one of the constraints in (\ref{eq:WHAs2}, \ref{eq:WHAs3}) fails
for such $I_{j}$'s. We discuss the possibilities as follows.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) \uline{\mbox{$\omega_{I_{j}}>\delta$}.} 

\vspace{2mm} Since $\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M$, one has 
\[
\delta^{p}\cdot\big|\{j:\omega_{I_{j}}>\delta\}\big|\leqslant\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{p}\leqslant M^{p}.
\]
As a result, 
\begin{equation}
\big|\{j:\omega_{I_{j}}>\delta\}\big|\leqslant\delta^{-p}M^{p}.\label{eq:C1}
\end{equation}
(ii) \uline{\mbox{$l_{I_{j}}>\gamma_{0}a_{j}/2$}.}

\vspace{2mm} Since $a_{j}\geqslant R/2$, one has 
\[
\frac{\gamma_{0}R}{4}\cdot\big|\{j:l_{I_{j}}>\gamma_{0}a_{j}/2\}\big|\leqslant\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}l_{I_{j}}\leqslant\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}.
\]
Therefore, 
\begin{equation}
\big|\{j:l_{I_{j}}>\gamma_{0}a_{j}/2\}\big|\leqslant\frac{4\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}}{\gamma_{0}R}.\label{eq:C2}
\end{equation}
(iii) \uline{\mbox{$\Xi_{I_{j}}>\eta_{0}$}.} 

\vspace{2mm} By definition, one has 
\begin{equation}
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\Xi_{I_{j}}\leqslant\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{1+\theta}.\label{eq:SumXi}
\end{equation}
The first sum in (\ref{eq:SumXi}) is estimated as 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}\leqslant N_{R}^{1-1/p}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{p}\Big)^{1/p}\leqslant MN_{R}^{1-1/p}.
\]
For the second sum in (\ref{eq:SumXi}), one can first use H\"older's
inequality to obtain that 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta}\leqslant M\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta p'}\Big)^{1/p'}.
\]
Next, observe that $\theta p'>1$. Since the $l^{p}$-norm is nonincreasing
in $p$, one has 
\[
\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta p'}\Big)^{1/p'}\leqslant\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}l_{I_{j}}\Big)^{\theta}\leqslant\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}^{\theta}.
\]
As a consequence, 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}l_{I_{j}}^{\theta}\leqslant M\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}^{\theta}.
\]
The last sum in (\ref{eq:SumXi}) again easily estimated by monotonicity
of $l^{p}$-norm; since $1+\theta>p$, one has 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{1+\theta}\leqslant\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\omega_{I_{j}}^{p}\Big)^{\frac{1+\theta}{p}}\leqslant M^{1+\theta}.
\]
To summarise, one concludes that 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N_{R}}\Xi_{I_{j}}\leqslant M\Big(\frac{R}{6\pi}\Big)^{1-1/p}+M\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}^{\theta}+M^{1+\theta}.
\]
It follows that 
\begin{equation}
\big|\{j:\Xi_{I_{j}}>\eta_{0}\}\big|\leqslant\eta_{0}^{-1}\Big[M\Big(\frac{R}{6\pi}\Big)^{1-1/p}+M\|h\|_{1\text{-var}}^{\theta}+M^{1+\theta}\Big].\label{eq:C3}
\end{equation}
The number of $j$'s such that $I_{j}$ does not contain an $(a_{0},\theta_{0})$-effective
turn is therefore bounded above by the sum of the RHS of (\ref{eq:C1},
\ref{eq:C2}, \ref{eq:C3}). Since $N_{R}=\frac{R}{6\pi}$, this immediately
yields a lower bound of ${\cal N}_{{\rm eff}}(h)$ in the form of
(\ref{eq:TurnEstPert}). The proof of Lemma \ref{lem:TurnEstPert}
is now complete.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $({\cal W},\bar{{\cal H}},\mu)$ be the abstract Wiener space
associated with the 2D fBM (in particular, $\mu$ is the law of fBM).
Fix $p\in(1/H)^{+}$ as before and fix $M>0$ (its precise value is
of no importance). Define
\[
G_{M}:=\big\{ w\in{\cal W}:\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M\big\}.
\]
For each $R>0,$ we also set 
\[
A_{R}:=\Big\{ w\in{\cal W}:\sup_{0\leqslant t\leqslant1}|X_{t}^{w}|>R\Big\}
\]
According to Proposition \ref{prop:KeyCoer}, there exist positive
constants $c_{0},R_{0},$ such that 
\[
G_{M}+c_{0}R^{H+1/2}{\cal K}\subseteq A_{R}^{c}
\]
for all $R>R_{0},$ where ${\cal K}$ denotes the closed unit ball
of $\bar{{\cal H}}.$ Let 
\[
\kappa:=\Phi^{-1}(\mu(G_{M}))\in\mathbb{R},
\]
where $\Phi(u):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{x}e^{-u^{2}/2}du$.
It follows from Borell's isoperimetric inequality (see \cite[Theorem 4.3]{Led94})
that 
\begin{align*}
\mu(A_{R}) & =1-\mu(A_{R}^{c})\leqslant1-\mu\big(G_{M}+c_{0}R^{H+1/2}{\cal K}\big)\\
 & \leqslant1-\Phi(\kappa+c_{0}R^{H+1/2})\leqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2H+1}}
\end{align*}
for all $R>R_{0}$ with suitable constants $C_{1},C_{2}>0.$ This
completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:2DCounter}.

label: thm:GLowH
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm:GLowH}Let $H\in(1/2,1)$ and $V_0,V_1,\cdots,V_d\in C_b^2$. Suppose that Condition (H) holds. Then there exist
positive constants $C_{1},C_{2}$ depending only on $H$ and the vector fields, such that
the estimate
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(\big|X_{1}-x_{0}\big|>R\big)\geqslant C_{1}e^{-C_{2}R^{2}}
\]
holds for all large $R$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As usual, we use $X_{t}^{w}$ to denote the solution to the same equation
(\ref{eq:SDEIntro}) with $B_{t}$ replaced by $w_{t}$. Given $R>0,$
we set $h_{t}^{R}:=Rt\eta$ ($0\leqslant t\leqslant1$) where $\eta$
is the unit vector given by Condition (H). This particular Cameron-Martin
path will play a critical role in the argument. Let $F$ be the function
given by Condition (H).

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) The key claim is that there exist positive
constants $M,C_{0},R_{0}$ depending only on $p,H,V,F$, such that
\begin{equation}
\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M\implies\big|X_{1}^{w+h^{R}}-x\big|\geqslant C_{0}R\label{eq:DispEstYoung}
\end{equation}
for all $R>R_{0}.$ 

To prove this claim, let us write $X_{t}:=X_{t}^{w+h^{R}}$ and $V=(V_{1},\cdots,V_{d})$
for simplicity. Note that $X_{t}$ satisfies the following equation:
\[
dX_{t}=RW_{\eta}(X_{t})dt+V(X_{t})dw_{t}+V_{0}(X_{t})dt.
\]
Let $F$ be the function given by Condition (H). By applying the chain
rule to $F(X_{t})$, one obtains that 
\begin{align*}
F(X_{1})-F(x_{0})= & R\int_{0}^{1}(W_{\eta}F)(X_{t})dt+\int_{0}^{1}\big(\nabla F(X_{t})\big)^{T}V(X_{t})dw_{t}\\
 & \ \ \ +\int_{0}^{1}\big(\nabla F(X_{t})\big)^{T}V_{0}(X_{t})dt=:A+B+C.
\end{align*}
According to Condition (H), one has $A\geqslant mR$. It is also obvious
that $|C|\leqslant\|DF\|_{\infty}\|V_{0}\|_{\infty}.$ 

To estimate $B$, let us set 
\[
x_{I}:=\|X\|_{p\text{-var};I},\quad\omega_{I}:=\|\omega\|_{p\text{-var};I}
\]
for any given interval $I\subseteq[0,1]$. By using \cite[Theorem 6.8]{FV10},
one easily finds that 
\[
x_{I}\leqslant\big(R\|V\|_{\infty}+\|V_{0}\|_{\infty}\big)|I|+C_{p}\big(\|V\|_{\infty}+\|DV\|_{\infty}x_{I}\big)\omega_{I}.
\]
Let $M$ be chosen such that 
\[
C_{p}\|DV\|_{\infty}M<\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Whenever $\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M$, one has 
\begin{equation}
x_{I}\leqslant2\big(R\|V\|_{\infty}+\|V_{0}\|_{\infty}\big)|I|+2C_{p}\|V\|_{\infty}M.\label{eq:xIEst}
\end{equation}
Now we divide the interval $[0,1]$ into equal subintervals $I_{1},\cdots,I_{N}$
($N\asymp R$) each having length $1/R$. According to (\ref{eq:xIEst}),
on each subinterval $I_{j}$ one has 
\begin{equation}
x_{I_{j}}\leqslant C_{p,V}\label{eq:xIjEst}
\end{equation}
with some constant $C_{p,V}$ depending on $p,V.$ It follows
again from \cite[Theorem 6.8]{FV10} and (\ref{eq:xIjEst}) that 
\begin{align*}
|B| & \leqslant\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Big|\int_{I_{j}}\big(\nabla F(X_{t})\big)^{T}V(X_{t})dw_{t}\Big|\\
 & \leqslant C_{p}\big(\|(\nabla F)^{T}\cdot V\|_{\infty}+C_{p,V}\big\|D\big((\nabla F)^{T}\cdot V\big)\big\|_\infty\big)\sum_{j=1}^{N}\omega_{I_{i}}\\
 & \leqslant C'_{p,V,F}R^{1-1/p}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N}\omega_{I_{j}}^{p}\Big)^{1/p}\\
 & \leqslant C'_{p,V,F}MR^{1-1/p}.
\end{align*}
As a consequence, 
\begin{align*}
\|\nabla F\|_{\infty}|X_{1}-x_{0}| & \geqslant F(X_{1})-F(x_{0})\\
 & \geqslant mR-C'_{p,V,F}MR^{1-1/p}-\|DF\|_{\infty}\|V_{0}\|_{\infty}.
\end{align*}
Let $R_{0}$ be chosen such that the RHS is larger than $mR/2$ for
all $R>R_{0}.$ The claim (\ref{eq:DispEstYoung}) thus follows with
$C_{0}:=\frac{m}{2\|\nabla F\|_{\infty}}.$

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) The claim (\ref{eq:DispEstYoung}) shows
that 
\[
G_{M}:=\big\{ w:\|w\|_{p\text{-var}}\leqslant M\big\}\subseteq\Big\{\big|X_{1}^{w+h^{R}}-x_{0}\big|\geqslant C_{0}R\Big\}
\]
for all $R>R_{0}.$ As a consequence, 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(\big|X_{1}^{B}-x_{0}\big|\geqslant C_{0}R\big)\geqslant\mu(h^{R}+G_{M}),
\]
where $\mu$ is the law of fBM on path space. By exactly the same
Cameron-Martin transformation argument as in the proof of Theorem
\ref{thm:RoughLowG}, one finds that 
\[
\mu(h^{R}+G_{M})=e^{-\|h^{R}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}\big[e^{-\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle}{\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\big].
\]
Here $\theta^{R}:=K_{H}^{-1}h^{R}\in L^{2}([0,1];\mathbb{R}^{d})$
($K_{H}$ is the isomorphism defined by (\ref{eq:KHIso})) and $W$
is the Wiener process in the fBM representation (\ref{eq:fBMRep}).
By the definition of $h^{R},$ it is obvious that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hRNorm}
\|h^{R}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}=R\|[t\mapsto t\eta]\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}=:\kappa R.
\end{equation}
In addition, due to the reflection symmetry of the set $G_{M}$, one
has 
\[
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{-\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle}{\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle}{\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\big].
\]
In particular, 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{-\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle}{\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\big] & =\mathbb{E}\Big[\cosh\Big(\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta_{t}^{R},dW_{t}\rangle\Big){\bf 1}_{G_{M}}(B)\Big]\\
 & \geqslant\mu(G_{M}):=\delta.
\end{align*}
As a result, one concludes that 
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(\big|X_{1}^{B}-x_{0}\big|\geqslant C_{0}R\big)\geqslant\delta e^{-\kappa^{2}R^{2}/2}
\]
for all $R>R_{0}$. 

Now the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GLowH} is complete.

label: eq:CtyEstGenLowYoung
title: Proof
body_md:
The argument is a simple adaptation of the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GLowH}.
It is more convenient to use H\"older norms here. Fix a unit vector
$\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ and $\rho\in(1/2,H)$. Given $R>1$, let
$X_{t}^{R}$ denote the solution to the differential equation 
\[
dX_{t}^{R}=R\eta dt+V(X_{t}^{R})dB_{t}+V_{0}(X_{t}^{R})dt,\quad X_{0}^{R}=x_{0}.
\]
Similar to Part (i) of the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GLowH} with
$p$-variation replaced by $\rho$-H\"older norm (cf. Lemma \ref{lem:LinDisplace}),
there exist positive constants $M,C_{1},C_{2},R_{0},$ such that on
the event 
\[
A_{M}:=\big\{\|B\|_{\rho\text{-H\"ol};[0,1]}\leqslant M\big\},
\]
the estimates
\begin{equation}
\big|X_{t}^{R}-X_{s}^{R}\big|\leqslant C_{1}\big(R|t-s|+M|t-s|^{\rho}+|t-s|\big)\label{eq:CtyEstGenLowYoung}
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}
|X_{1}^{R,w}-x_{0}|\geqslant C_{2}R\label{eq:GloDispGenYoung}
\end{equation}
hold for all $R>R_{0}$ and $s,t\in[0,1]$. 

Now let us define the (random) Cameron-Martin path
\[
h_{t}^{R}:=R\int_{0}^{t}a(X_{s}^{R})ds,
\]
where $a(x):=A(x)\eta$ and $A(x)$ is the right inverse of $V(x)$
defined by (\ref{eq:RightInv}). Note that $h^{R}$ is ${\cal F}^{W}$-adapted
(cf. (\ref{eq:fBMRep})). According to the norm-equivalence relation
(\ref{eq:EquivFracNorm}), one has 
\begin{align*}
\|h^{R}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}^{2} & \leqslant C_{H}\Big(\|\dot{h}^{R}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{|\dot{h}_{t}^{R}-\dot{h}_{s}^{R}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{2H}}dsdt\Big)\\
 & =C_{H}R^{2}\Big(\|u^{R}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{|\dot{u}_{t}^{R}-\dot{u}_{s}^{R}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{2H}}dsdt\Big)
\end{align*}
where $u_{t}^{R}:=a(X_{t}^{R})$. The $L^{2}$-norm in the first term
is uniformly bounded by $\|A\|_{\infty}$. For the second term, by
using (\ref{eq:CtyEstGenLowYoung}) one easily finds that 
\[
\big|u_{t}^{R}-u_{s}^{R}\big|\leqslant C_{3}\big(\min\{1,R|t-s|\}+M|t-s|^{\rho}\big)
\]
for all $R>R_{0}$ and $s,t\in[0,1]$. It follows from explicit analysis
that 
\begin{align*}
 & \int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{|\dot{u}_{t}^{R}-\dot{u}_{s}^{R}|^{2}}{|t-s|^{2H}}dsdt\\
 & \leqslant C_{3}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\Big(\frac{\min\{1,R^{2}|t-s|^{2}\}}{|t-s|^{2H}}+M|t-s|^{2\rho-2H}\Big)\\
 & \leqslant C_{4}R^{2H-1}
\end{align*}
on the event $A_{M}.$ As a consequence, 
\begin{equation}
\|h^{R}\|_{\bar{{\cal H}}}^{2}\leqslant C_{H}R^{2}\big(\|A\|_{\infty}^{2}+C_{4}R^{2H-1}\big)\leqslant C_{5}R^{2H+1}\label{eq:CMGenYoung}
\end{equation}
on $A_{M}.$

Let \[\tau:=\inf\big\{t\geqslant 0:\|B\|_{\rho\text{-H\"ol};[0,t]}>M\big\}\wedge 1\] and define 
\[\hat{h}^R_t := R\int_{0}^{t\wedge \tau}a(X_{s}^{R})ds.\]Note that $\hat{h}^R$ is also $\mathcal{F}^W$-adapted and $\hat{h}^R = h^R$ on $A_M$. From the above analysis, it is not hard to see that with probability one, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:CMGenYoung}
\big\|\dot{\hat{h}}^R\big\|_{\bar{\cal H}}\leqslant C_6 R^{2H+1}
\end{equation}for all $R$. With the global Cameron-Martin estimate (\ref{eq:CMGenYoung}), one can now carry through the Cameron-Martin transformation argument as in the
proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GLowH} (cf. the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:RoughLowG}) to conclude the desired $(2H+1)$-Weibull
lower bound (\ref{eq:WeibullGenYoung}).

label: def:Folia
title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
\label{def:Folia}
Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional differentiable manifold. Let ${\cal F}$
be a collection of immersed $k$-dimensional submanifolds. A chart
$(U,\varphi)$ is said to be \textit{flat} for ${\cal F}$ if the
following two properties hold:

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) $\varphi(U)$ is a cube in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$;

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) for each submanifold $N\in{\cal F}$ with
nonempty intersection with $U$, the set $\varphi(N\cap U)$ is a
countable union of $k$-dimensional slices of the form 
\[
x^{k+1}=c^{k+1},\cdots,x^{n}=c^{n}
\]
in $\varphi(U).$ 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent A \textit{$k$-dimensional (smooth) foliation}
on $M$ is a collection ${\cal F}$ of disjoint, connected, immersed
$k$-dimensional submanifolds such that the union of members of ${\cal F}$
is $M$ and for every $x\in M$, there exists a chart around $x$
which is flat for ${\cal F}.$ Members of a foliation ${\cal F}$
are called \textit{leaves} of ${\cal F}.$

title: \protect\examplename
body_md:
Let $M$ be a closed surface. Let $W$ be a smooth vector field on
$M$ which is everywhere nonvanishing. According to the global Frobenius
theorem, the integral curves of $W$ form a one-dimensional (1D) foliation
on $M$ (see \cite[Theorem 19.21]{Lee13}). This is the main example
that is relevant to us.

label: def:Reeb
title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
\label{def:Reeb}

Let ${\cal F}$ be a 1D foliation on $\mathbb{T}^{2}.$ We say that
${\cal F}$ \textit{has a Reeb component} if there exists an embedded
annulus $A\cong S^{1}\times[0,1]$ inside $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ such that:

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) $\partial A$ is the union of two compact
leaves of ${\cal F}$ that are in opposite homotopy classes;

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) there are no compact leaves of ${\cal F}$
in the interior of $A$.

Let ${\cal F},{\cal F}'$ be $k$-dimensional foliations on $n$-dimensional

label: thm:1DFoliClass
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm:1DFoliClass}Let ${\cal F}$ be a 1D foliation on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$.
Then either ${\cal F}$ has a Reeb component or it is conjugate to
the suspension of an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:S^{1}\rightarrow S^{1}$.
head: environment

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
For each $x\in\mathbb{T}^{2},$ the set $\{\phi_{t}(x):t\in\mathbb{R}\}$
is called the \textit{orbit} of $W$ through $x$. An orbit $\gamma$
is said to be \textit{periodic} if there exist $T>0$ and $x\in\gamma$
(equivalently, for all $x\in\gamma$) such that $\phi_{T}(x)=x$.
The smallest positive number satisfying the above relation is called
the \textit{period} of $\gamma$. A periodic orbit is \textit{noncontractible}
if its homology class in $H_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2};\mathbb{Z})$ is nonzero.
head: environment

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
The map $P$ constructed above is known as the \textit{Poincar\'e
map} at $x\in\gamma$ with respect to the transversal $\Sigma$.
The number $\lambda_{\gamma}$ is called the \textit{transverse characteristic
number} of $\gamma.$
head: environment

label: def:HypOrb
title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
\label{def:HypOrb}Let $\gamma$ be a periodic orbit of a smooth,
everywhere nonvanishing vector field $W$ on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$. We
say that $\gamma$ is \textit{hyperbolic} if $\lambda_{\gamma}\neq1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We
therefore assume that there exists a diffeomorphism $\Psi:\mathbb{T}^{2}\rightarrow\Sigma_{f}$,
where $\Sigma_{f}$ is the suspension of an orientation-preserving
diffeomorphism $f:S^{1}\rightarrow S^{1},$ such that $\Psi({\cal F}_{\alpha_{0}})={\cal F}_{f}$
(see Definition \ref{def:Suspension} and Definition \ref{def:Conj}). 

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) Consider the projection 
\[
\rho:\Sigma_{f}\rightarrow S^{1}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z},\quad\rho([x,t])\mapsto t\ \ ({\rm mod}\ \mathbb{Z}).
\]
Let $d\theta$ denote the canonical volume form on $S^{1}$ such that
$\int_{S^{1}}d\theta=1$. Define the closed $1$-form $\beta:=\rho^{*}(d\theta)$
on $\Sigma_{f}.$ Let $Y$ be the suspension vector field on $\Sigma_{f}$;
the vertical vector field $\partial_{t}$ on $S^{1}\times\mathbb{R}$
descends to $Y$ on $\Sigma_{f}$ under the quotient of the $\mathbb{Z}$-action
(\ref{eq:ZActSusp}), which is tangential to the foliation ${\cal F}_{f}$.
By definition, one has 
\[
\langle\beta(\xi),Y(\xi)\rangle=\langle d\theta,(d\rho)(Y)\rangle_{\rho(\xi)}=\langle d\theta,\partial_{t}\rangle_{\rho(\xi)}=1
\]
for every $\xi\in\Sigma_{f}$.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Since $\Psi({\cal F}_{\alpha_{0}})={\cal F}_{f}$,
there exists a nonvanishing function $\lambda\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$
such that
\[
(d\Psi)_{x}(W_{\alpha_{0}}(x))=\lambda(x)Y(\Psi(x))
\]
for every $x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}.$ By connectedness, one may assume without loss of generality that 
\[
m:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}}\lambda(x)>0.
\]
Let $\eta:=\Psi^{*}(\beta).$ It follows that $\eta$ is closed and
one has 
\[
\langle\eta(x),W_{\alpha_{0}}(x)\rangle=\lambda(x)\langle\beta(\Psi(x)),Y(\Psi(x))\rangle=\lambda(x)
\]
for every $x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}.$ In particular, 
\begin{equation}
\inf_{x\in\mathbb{T}^{2}}\langle\eta(x),W_{\alpha_{0}}(x)\rangle=m>0.\label{eq:NonDegEta}
\end{equation}
(iii) We claim that the (de Rham) cohomology class $[\eta]$ is nontrivial.
Indeed, if $\eta$ were exact, say $\eta=dq$ for some $q\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$,
one would have $\eta(x^{*})=0$ at the location $x^{*}$ where $q$
is maximised. This contradicts the fact (\ref{eq:NonDegEta}). Therefore,
$[\eta]\neq0.$

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (iv) Let $[\alpha_{1}],[\alpha_{2}]$ denote
a basis of $H_{1}(\Sigma_{f};\mathbb{Z})$ such that 
\begin{equation}
\int_{[\alpha_{1}]}[\beta]=0,\quad\int_{[\alpha_{2}]}[\beta]=1.\label{eq:BetaBasis}
\end{equation}
One can construct them in the following way. The loop $\alpha_{1}=([x,t])_{x\in S^{1}}$
is a circle positively winding around the horizontal $S^{1}$-component
once. The loop $\alpha_{2}$ is defined by a vertical curve $\alpha_{2}':=[(x,t)]_{0\leqslant t\leqslant1}$
concatenated with a horizontal arc $\alpha_{2}''$ joining $[(f(x),0)]$
back to $[(x,0)]$ along the horizontal $S^{1}$-component. This concatenation
is needed since $\alpha_{2}'$ may fail to be a closed curve (leaves
of ${\cal F}_{f}$ needs not be compact). The relation (\ref{eq:BetaBasis})
is now obvious from the construction. 

Let $\{[l_{1}],[l_{2}]\}$ be the canonical basis of $H_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2};\mathbb{Z})$
that is dual to $\{[dx^{1}],[dx^{2}]\}$. Let $\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2}$
be the preimages of $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}$ under the diffeomorphism
$\Psi$. Then $\{[\zeta_{1}],[\zeta_{2}]\}$ is a basis of $H_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2};\mathbb{Z})$
and one has 
\[
\int_{[\zeta_{1}]}[\eta]=0,\quad\int_{[\zeta_{2}]}[\eta]=1.
\]
In particular, one can write 
\[
[\zeta_{1}]=a[l_{1}]+b[l_{2}],\quad[\zeta_{2}]=c[l_{1}]+d[l_{2}]
\]
with some matrix 
\[
A=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
a & b\\
c & d
\end{array}\right)\in{\rm GL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z}).
\]
It follows that 
\[
[\eta]=k_{1}[dx^{1}]+k_{2}[dx^{2}],
\]
where 
\[
\left(\begin{array}{c}
k_{1}\\
k_{2}
\end{array}\right):=A^{-1}\cdot\left(\begin{array}{c}
0\\
1
\end{array}\right)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\backslash\{(0,0)\}.
\]
As a result, one has
\[
\eta=k_{1}dx^{1}+k_{2}dx^{2}+d\varphi
\]
for some $\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2}).$

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (v) Consider the function 
\[
F(x^{1},x^{2}):=k_{1}x^{1}+k_{2}x^{2}+\tilde{\varphi}(x^{1},x^{2}),\quad x=(x^{1},x^{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2},
\]
where $\tilde{\varphi}$ is the pullback of $\varphi$ (i.e. its periodic
extension) on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. It is clear that $F$ has bounded
first and second derivatives on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. In addition, let
$\eta:=(\cos\alpha_{0},\sin\alpha_{0})^{T}$ and let $\tilde{V}$
be the periodic extension of $V$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ (same for $\tilde{W}_{\alpha_{0}}$).
Then one has 
\[
((\tilde{V}\cdot\eta)F)(x)=\langle dF(x),\tilde{W}_{\alpha_{0}}(x)\rangle=\langle\eta([x]),W_{\alpha_{0}}([x])\rangle\geqslant m>0
\]
for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ ($[x]\in\mathbb{T}^{2}$ denotes the
projected image of $x$). As a consequence, Condition (H) in Section
\ref{sec:LowGauCondYoung} is satisfied with the above choices of
$\eta$ and $F$. The Gaussian lower tail estimate (\ref{eq:GaussLowTorus})
now follows from Theorem {\ref{thm:GLowH}}.

title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem:HyperSelect}Let $\alpha_{0}\in[0,2\pi)$ be such that
the foliation of $W_{\alpha_{0}}$ contains a Reeb component. Then
there exists $\alpha_{*}\in[0,2\pi)$ such that $W_{\alpha_{*}}$
admits a hyperbolic periodic orbit.
